newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra urges business to exploit Japanese reform.
newsitem.headline: Canberra urges business to exploit Japanese reform.

text.p: The Australian government urged business on Wednesday to exploit Japanese economic deregulation and look for new trade opportunities in Japan, traditionally a tough market to penetrate but still the largest economy in Asia.
"Take another look at Japan," the Foreign Affairs Department told companies. "It could mean big business."

The Japanese business environment was expensive and challenging but things were changing, the department's East Asia Analytical Unit said in a report on the country that is already Australia's largest trading partner.
"Regulation is being reduced and becoming more transparent, and business practices are becoming less opaque.
"Consumer tastes are changing, making foreign products easier to sell."

Japan has been Australia's biggest trade partner since the 1960s. Thanks to vast shipments of bulk commodities such as coal and iron ore, Australia is one of the few countries that maintains a trade surplus with Japan.
But Australia's share of the Japanese market is slipping as raw materials account for less and less of Japan's imports.
The department estimated that Australia's share of Japanese imports declined to 4.8 percent in 1996 from 5.8 percent in 1985.
So Australia had to turn its attention to selling manufactures and services to Japan -- and Japanese deregulation would make that easier.
"While ... commodity trade remains vital to Australia, excellent opportunities exist to tap into Japan's fast-growing demand for high-value-added products," it said.
"Processed foods, housing and construction materials, alcoholic beverages, jewellery, fashion apparel, even refined copper, are growth segments in which Australia has comparative advantage."
Even the process of economic reform itself was an opportunity.
Japan's attempts to bypass clogged roads with coastal shipping presented an opportunity for Australia's fast-ferry builders.
Australia's traditional resources exports would benefit if Japan could reform its energy distribution system, cut prices and thereby boost demand.
The department estimated that Japan could sustain three percent annual growth in gross domestic product if it reformed its economy.
"With slower reform, growth probably would not surpass 1.5 percent per year."
